::: {.lead}
Before Byte Bay submits *Pocket Quest*, the producer asks Rami: "Will it
pass the review?" The answer is in the stores' **guidelines**: Apple's App
Review Guidelines and the Google Play Developer Policy. They are long, but
they have a clear structure, and most rejections come from a few common
problems. In lecture 17 you followed the road to the store. In this seminar
you **read** the guidelines like a reviewer: you learn their main parts,
you sort real problems into them, you decide like a reviewer, and you build
your own checklist. Every section ends with a task, and at the end you have
a pre-submission checklist for a game.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary store-guidelines app-review in-app-purchase loot-box privacy-policy age-rating store-listing >}}

## 18.1 The main parts of the guidelines

Apple's App Review Guidelines have five parts; the Google Play Developer
Policy covers the same topics in its own order (@fig-parts).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 18.1 — The five parts"}
- **Safety:** objectionable content, children, chat and user-generated
  content.
- **Performance:** a complete build without crashes, a true listing.
- **Business:** in-app purchases, ads, loot boxes and their odds.
- **Design:** no copies or spam, enough features.
- **Legal:** privacy and data, intellectual property.
:::

![The main parts of the store guidelines.](images/guideline-parts.png){#fig-parts width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 18.1 — Where is the rule?"}
1. Pocket Quest sells gems: **Business** (in-app purchases).
2. It has a chat between players: **Safety** (user-generated content).
3. It saves the player's e-mail: **Legal** (privacy).
:::

{{< sim file="sims/guideline-sorter.html" poster="sims/guideline-sorter.png" title="Guideline Sorter: which part of the rules?" height="520" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading a copy of the guidelines on another website, or an old summary.
The stores change the rules several times a year: read the official page
and note its date.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the parts"}
1. Open the official App Review Guidelines (developer.apple.com) or the
   Google Play Developer Policy Center. Find the part about in-app purchases.
2. In **Guideline Sorter**, sort all nine problems.

*Your result:* the title and date of the page, and your score.
:::

## 18.2 Common reasons for a rejection

Most games are not rejected for unusual reasons, but for a few common
problems (@fig-reasons).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 18.2 — Six common reasons"}
1. **Crashes and bugs** on the reviewer's devices.
2. **Incomplete build:** placeholders, "coming soon", an empty shop.
3. **Misleading listing:** screenshots or texts that do not match the game.
4. **Privacy:** no policy, data collected without a reason, too many
   permissions.
5. **Payments:** digital items not sold through the store, loot-box odds
   not shown.
6. **Other people's content:** music, art, characters or brands without a
   licence.
:::

![Six common reasons for a rejection.](images/rejection-reasons.png){#fig-reasons width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 18.2 — Gem Rush is rejected"}
*Gem Rush* sells a mystery chest for 2 USD with random gems, and the odds
are not shown.

1. Part: **Business** (loot boxes).
2. The rule: show the odds of each item before the purchase.
3. The fix: a small "odds" button on the chest screen, then a new
   submission.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Arguing with the review instead of reading the named rule. The rejection
message names the guideline: read it, fix the problem, and answer clearly
in the reply.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Judge two games"}
For two games you know, find one rule of the guidelines that each must
follow (for example its purchases or its chat). Write the part and the
rule.

*Your result:* two parts and two rules.
:::

## 18.3 A pre-submission checklist

A checklist turns the guidelines into simple questions that a studio asks
before every upload (@fig-check).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 18.3 — A pre-submission checklist"}
A **pre-submission checklist** has one line for each common reason and each
part of the guidelines that fits the game. Each line is a yes-or-no
question, checked before every new build.
:::

![A pre-submission checklist for Pocket Quest.](images/checklist.png){#fig-check width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 18.3 — Two lines checked"}
1. "Every button works; no 'coming soon'." Rami finds a button "Clans
   (soon)". He hides it until the feature is ready.
2. "Licences and credits for all music, art and fonts." The menu music came
   from a website without a licence. Byte Bay replaces it with music it
   made itself.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A checklist from another game copied without thinking. A game without
purchases needs no line for loot boxes, but a game with chat needs lines for
reporting and blocking.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your checklist"}
Write a checklist of at least eight lines for a game you know or plan.
Name the part of the guidelines for each line.

*Your result:* a checklist with eight lines.
:::

## Case study: Review Board

Today Rami plays the reviewer. Six games wait: *Pocket Quest 1.0*, tested
and complete; *Sky Farm*, with "coming soon" buttons and an empty shop;
*Gem Rush*, with a mystery chest and no odds; *Hero Wars X*, with the heroes
of a famous film series; *Tiny Chat Pets*, a game for children with free
chat; and *Speed Car 3*, which crashes on start. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses these games. In the mini-game below you decide
for each one.

## Further reading

Apple Developer, "App Review Guidelines"; Google Play Console Help,
"Developer Program Policy" and "Policy Center". Read the official, dated
versions.

## Exercises

1. Name the five parts of Apple's App Review Guidelines.
2. Which part covers a chat between players?
3. Which part covers the purchase of gems?
4. Which part covers a privacy policy?
5. Name three common reasons for a rejection.
6. What must a game with loot boxes show?
7. Why is a "coming soon" button a problem?
8. Why read the official page and not a summary?
9. What is a pre-submission checklist?
10. A game uses the music of a famous band without a licence. Which part,
    and what is the fix?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Safety, Performance, Business, Design, Legal.
2. Safety.
3. Business.
4. Legal.
5. For example crashes, an incomplete build, a misleading listing.
6. The odds of each item, before the purchase.
7. The build is incomplete: it shows features that do not exist.
8. The rules change several times a year.
9. Yes-or-no questions from the guidelines, checked before every upload.
10. Legal (intellectual property); a licence, or music the studio owns.
:::
